To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

surveillance technology in long-term residential facilities for people with intellectual or dementia is perceived by clients as a means to increase their autonomy, but is also experienced as a means of control and as an intrusion on privacy.
clients in residential care settings experience surveillance technology as an intrusion on their autonomy, but also as a way to increase their freedom of movement and autonomy.

the experiences of clients in residential care with surveillance technology entail a pattern of two main themes: (1). coping with new spaces, which includes clients wandering around, getting “lost,” being triggered, and retreat to “new spaces”; and (2). resisting the surveillance technology measures because clients feel stigmatised, missed the company of others and do not like to be “watched.”
